title: In Lawrence of Arabia (1962), why does this superior ask Lawrence twice where he's going?

commenti.body: We're not given a precise reason, although the superior does say "we don't want chaps in here who should be on duty." The deeper point, however, is that this scene is there to make Lawrence seem a bit of a fish-out-of-water, as of yet in an endearing way, to the audience. It makes his turn to war hero a greater arc, and contrasts well both with his wanton bloodshed later on while also setting-up his thriller-seeker hamartia pretty subtly.

The superior simply doesn’t believe that an odd duck like Lawrence would have an audience with the general. When Lawrence says the pow wow line, the superior assumes he’s trying to be a smart-ass instead of answering a direct question, so he reinforces that he’s Secretary of the mess hall to get him to answer truthfully.

I think it shows the dynamic of the British in North Africa, where their fastidious arrogance slightly falters in this sparsely populated desert where people don't seem to even acknowledge the concept of one overall leader. All the hemming-and-hawing bureaucratic contempt is there but it's just...kinda loose, isn't it? Lawrence isn't *really* the only person shuffling around idly, even if his superiors try to make him feel cornered. Hell, even the stern-but-ultimately-wise general's actual insight was that their status quo fucking sucked.

I think it also shows that Lawrence, despite being very self-possessed, doesn't have a solid sense of what he's good at or even believes in. The biggest insight is that his idea of 'adventure' is learning about the various peoples of the land, even at risk of death.

We need to see that early Lawrence *'can't help himself'* so the big moments where he fully knows the risks and walks back into the desert or foregoes his pacifism really hit. He's not just a guy who entered a warzone with a quirky humanistic perspective, he's a unique person who learns lessons, some flawed, and continues to reflect on his morals while shifting from a passive thinker to a self-sacrificing man of action.

The overall point is that he doesn't "fit in". He doesn't dress, speak or act like the other officers. Nobody knows what he's doing, they don't understand him and they think he's some sort of oddball. Then he's later treated as hero by the same people who are dismissive of him.

When he *does* try, they basically laugh at him behind his back "lays it on a bit thick, what" or he's dismissed as a filthy w\*g, which to me is the best one-two punch in the entire film.
